body_ar:
حكم النظر إلى المحرمات أثناء الصوم ما الحكم في صوم شخص يظل ويبيت مشتغلا بالنظر في التلفزة وفيها النساء المتبرجات؟

هذا لم يصم في الواقع الصوم الذي يزيد إيمانه ويزيد تقواه، وإنما صام عن المباحات واشتغل بالمحرمات نسأل الله السلامة والعافية، فعلى الإنسان أن يتقي الله في بصره وأن يتذكر قول الله تعالى: {قل للمؤمنين يغضوا من أبصارهم ويحفظوا فروجهم ذلك أزكى لهم إن الله خبير بما يصنعون} فعلى الإنسان أن يغض من بصره وأن يحفظ فرجه، وأن يعلم أن البصر بريد الفرج، فما ينظر إليه يدخل فتنة في قلبه قد يصعب عليه علاجها لو اهتدى إلى العلاج، نسأل الله أن يهدينا أجمعين لما يحب ويرضى، ولذلك قال ابن القيم رحمه الله:
body_en:
The ruling on looking at forbidden things while fasting. What is the ruling on the fast of a person who spends his day and his night occupied with looking at the television, on which there are women who display themselves?

This person has not in reality fasted the fast that increases his faith and increases his God-consciousness. He has merely fasted from the permissible things and occupied himself with the forbidden ones. We ask God for safety and well-being. A person must fear God with regard to his sight, and must remember the words of God, exalted: {Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and to guard their private parts; that is purer for them. Indeed God is aware of what they do} (Sūrat al-Nūr 24:30). So a person must lower his gaze and guard his private parts, and must know that the eye is the courier of the loins: what he looks at brings a trial into his heart which it may be hard for him to cure, even were he guided to the cure. We ask God to guide us all to what He loves and is pleased with. That is why Ibn al-Qayyim, God have mercy on him, said:

flags.arabic: ولذلك قال ابن القيم رحمه الله:
flags.context: the last words of the published page
options: end the English on the colon, exactly where the Arabic ends
supply the lines of Ibn al-Qayyim that evidently followed
flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY — STYLE GUIDE §9. The page breaks off on a colon, in the middle of introducing a quotation from Ibn al-Qayyim which is then never given. The quoted lines are almost certainly the well-known verses on the glance, but they have NOT been supplied — restoring them from memory is exactly what the house rules forbid. The English ends on the same colon. Note also that the record's title announces general fatwas on fasting, in the plural, and only one is present before the break.

flags.arabic: هذا لم يصم في الواقع الصوم الذي يزيد إيمانه … وإنما صام عن المباحات واشتغل بالمحرمات
flags.context: the Sheikh's answer to the question about the validity of the fast
options: render faithfully and mark that the validity of the fast is not ruled on
render as a ruling that the fast is invalid
render as a ruling that the fast is valid but deficient
flags.note: CRITICAL. The question asks for the ruling on this person's fast. The Sheikh does not say that the fast is void (bāṭil) or defective (fāsid), and he does not say that it is valid. He says the man has not fasted the fast that increases faith and God-consciousness — a statement about the worth of the act, not its legal validity. The style guide's distinction between validity and moral status is exactly in play here: an act can be blameworthy and still valid. The English must not be allowed to answer the question the Sheikh left unanswered.

flags.context: the questioner's description, and the Sheikh's maxim
options: render both literally, as questioner's phrase and Sheikh's maxim respectively
render with the terms softened for a general readership
render with an added editorial frame
flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW. The questioner's phrase al-nisāʾ al-mutabarrijāt and the Sheikh's maxim that the eye is the courier of the loins are both blunt in Arabic and blunter still in English, and a passage of this kind about women's appearance carries reputational risk in some jurisdictions when read without its setting. Translated faithfully, neither softened nor strengthened. Note that the Qur'anic verse the Sheikh cites addresses believing men and their own gaze, and his application follows the verse rather than departing from it; nothing has been added.
